title: Effects of Short-Term Concurrent Training Cessation on the Energy Cost of Running and Neuromuscular Performances in Middle-Distance Runners
authors: Berryman N, Mujika I, Bosquet L
population: 8 middle-distance runners who completed an 8-week concurrent programme (4 added plyometric training, 4 added dynamic weight training) and then 4 weeks without explosive strength training while running was maintained
findings: The energy cost of running fell by 5.75% (95% CI -8.47 to -3.03) after the 8-week concurrent programme and was still lower after 4 weeks without explosive strength training (-6.31%, 95% CI -10.30 to -2.32).
Neuromuscular performances were maintained after the 4 weeks of cessation, especially in tests that were specific to the training intervention.

A 3000 m time trial improved after the concurrent mesocycle (-2.40%, 95% CI -4.65 to -0.16) and again after the cessation (-4.43%, 95% CI -6.83 to -2.03); only trivial changes were seen in aerobic endurance and VO2peak.

The authors suggest that short-term explosive strength training cessation could be considered as a taper strategy for middle-distance runners, and they caution that the sample is small and the literature very limited.
limitations: Eight runners, a case-report-type study with no control group, middle-distance runners and an explosive (not heavy) programme that was either plyometric or dynamic weights in four runners each; only 4 weeks of cessation, while running continued. Abstract read on Europe PMC (open access); full text not read.
implications: The only evidence in the corpus from runners on stopping strength work: the economy gain from an 8-week programme was kept for 4 weeks without it. It means a taper does not need a strength session to keep the gain over that span, and it does not support a cut of the lifting dose for a longer break or for heavy lifting.
Points the other way from the cyclists' result (ronnestad-2016-strength-cessation-cyclists); the taper rule keeps one light session as a default, not as a requirement.
